problem: Existing social navigation methods either group pedestrians by position/velocity (missing semantic interactions such as queuing or photographing) or query an LMM at every planning step, which is slow and gives uninterpretable behavior. Local planners also get stuck in local minima near groups.
motivation: Robots in human environments must avoid disturbing social groups such as queues, conversations and photo sessions, not just avoid collisions. LMMs have commonsense social reasoning but are too slow for high-frequency control, so they should be used only for low-frequency semantic grouping.
key_idea: Use a GPT-4o LMM with visual prompting (annotated image with masks and tracking IDs) at low frequency to zero-shot infer social groups, then feed the groups into a mid-level planner between global and local planning that reroutes around group social spaces.
insight: Semantic reasoning by LMMs is much better than proximity-based grouping: DBSCAN only reached 10.8-14.8% accurate grouping versus 77.8% for GPT-4o. Decoupling the slow LMM from high-frequency tracking and planning is workable. The mid-level planner matters: TEB with the same group estimate still gets stuck in local minima and disturbs groups more than GSON.
method: Pedestrian detection and tracking: fuses a DR-SPAAM 2D-LiDAR leg detector with YOLOv5 boxes by projecting detections into the image and keeping matched ones; Hungarian association plus a constant-velocity Kalman filter gives IDs, positions and velocities.

Visual-prompted group detection: annotates the image with boxes, segmentation masks and tracking IDs, queries gpt-4o-2024-08-06 with a structured prompt, and parses the output into group assignments stored in the tracker.
Keyframe querying: keeps the frame with the most visible people within a 1 s window and queries the LMM only when the keyframe updates or expires, reducing query frequency.
Global planner: A* with Jump Point Search on an inflated occupancy cost map.

Mid-level planner: computes the convex hull of each group and fits an ellipse as a social space. When the global path intersects it, a sub-goal is set a fixed arc length h past the last in-space waypoint, and BIT* replans only that segment to produce the CrowdFreePath.
Local planner: NMPC with control barrier functions tracks the CrowdFreePath and avoids pedestrians using constant-velocity predicted positions.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06, frozen; Qwen2.5-VL-32B also used in dense-crowd tests) + YOLOv5 + DR-SPAAM
setting.observation: two RGB cameras (merged image) + 2D LiDAR + SLAM pose, given occupancy map
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands for a differential-drive base (NMPC-CBF)
setting.privileged: pre-built 2D occupancy map of the environment; no other privileged information

numbers_note: Real-world navigation results (disturbance time, comfort distance, curvature, jerk, roughness, runtime) are given only in a bar chart figure, with no numeric table. LMM grouping accuracy is reported only for a custom 100-scenario set, not a standard navigation benchmark.
results: On real-robot scenarios (queuing, photographing, talking, walking), GSON has the lowest time disturbing individuals and groups and the highest comfort distance versus TEB, TEB+group estimate, SACSON, GMPC and RLCA. Traditional metrics stay comparable, with slightly higher jerk and runtime. GPT-4o gets 86.6% acceptable grouping (77.8% accurate + 8.8% miss) on 100 custom scenarios, versus 10.8-14.8% accurate for DBSCAN.
limitations: LMM latency (1.5-2 s with Qwen2.5-VL-32B, at least 1 s overall) reduces responsiveness in rapidly changing dense crowds.
Egocentric occlusions cause incomplete or wrong group detection.
Binary group labels and conservative avoidance of all groups lack nuanced social adaptation, e.g. crossing a queue versus interrupting a chat.
